newsitem.title: UK: EMS/Mark satellites plumb new lows in late Europe.
newsitem.headline: EMS/Mark satellites plumb new lows in late Europe.

text.p: The French franc slid to its worst level against the mark in over a month in late Europe as New York traders unleashed a fresh wave of selling on election and EMU uncertainties, dealers said.

The franc had fallen in early Europe -- pulling other mark satellites with it -- as speculation grew that French President Jacques Chirac would announce a snap election, seen as necessary to allow the government to push through austerity measures for France to qualify for the European single currency.
Chirac met his prime minister and parliamentary leaders this morning and will broadcast to the nation at 1800 GMT.
An early election "avoids the need to fight an election campaign next spring when EMU decisions will be taken," said David Coleman, chief economist at CIBC Wood Gundy in London.

Though the short term looked wobbly for the franc, analysts said the damage should not be huge. The likelihood that the centre-right coalition would retain power was also positive for the currency, they added.
The franc was quoted at 3.3768/71 per mark by 1351 GMT, down from late Friday's European level of 3.3694/99.
"I'm looking for 3.3800 -- I can't see a massive move," said Neal Kimberley, manager, EMS desk at Bank of Tokyo-Mitsubishi.

"There is going to be a single currency and France will certainly be a founder member of it, so at some point I expect convergence to move back onto the economic agenda," he said. Convergence was off the agenda on Monday, however, amid fears a Socialist-led French election victory would jeopardize austerity measures needed to meet EMU goals. Nagging worries over the monetary union prospects for high yielding currencies also weighed on the lira and the peseta.

An Italian parliamentary commission on Friday rejected a proposed mini-budget, designed to help Italy catch the first train to EMU in 1999, and made it likely a confidence vote would be needed to force the measure through.
Prime Minister Romano Prodi has staked his political career on EMU membership, vowing to resign if Italy does not make the grade.
At the weekend, Italian news agency ANSA reported that the International Monetary Fund had criticised the planned mini-budget for stressing EMU at the expense of structural reform.
"The big theme this week is renewed doubts about the EMU project," said Steve Hannah, director of research at IBJ here.
Those doubts had taken the shine off what should have been a sparkling week for Italy, with inflation data expected to be mild and paving the way for an interest rate cut, he said.
Preliminary Italian consumer price inflation figures for April were due out later on Monday and on Tuesday.

The lira sank to 993.20/50 per mark from Friday's European close of 988.40/90, while the Spanish peseta fell to 84.51/54 from 84.35/38 and Portugal's escudo hit its weakest point since December at 100./77/80 versus late Friday's 100.55/58.
Dealers said the Bank of Portugal had been buying escudos with increasing intensity to support its currency.
The market is now awaiting the European Commission's economic forecasts for member states in 1997/98, due Wednesday.

An EU source said last week that Italy would be predicted to miss the 3.0 percent deficit-to-GDP target for EMU, but newspaper reports have suggested the Commission's forecasts will indicate Germany and France meeting the 3.0 percent goal.
European Commissioner Emma Bonino, an Italian, said on Monday that she thought the document seemed "unbalanced".
Germany's six leading economic research institutes forecast the nation's public sector deficit at 3.0 to 3.2 percent of economic output, government sources said.
In a semiannual report to be released on Tuesday, the institutes said they had no doubt EMU would start on time in 1999 but criticised the fixation on the 3.0 percent budget deficit goal.
